report:
## Conclusion: Largely correct — with a nuance

For the general population, the answer is **no**: regular vitamin C intake does not meaningfully prevent colds. However, evidence shows a modest reduction in cold *duration/severity*, and a notable exception exists for people under extreme physical or cold stress.

**Evidence:**

The most authoritative source is the Cochrane systematic review (Hemilä & Chalker), which pooled 29 trial comparisons (11,306 participants). In the general community, regular vitamin C supplementation (≥0.2 g/day) had essentially no effect on cold incidence — pooled risk ratio 0.97 (95% CI 0.94–1.00), a statistically borderline and clinically trivial reduction ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23440782](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23440782/)). This directly refuted Linus Pauling's earlier claims that megadose vitamin C would prevent colds ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8078152](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8078152/)).

The same review found regular supplementation did shorten cold duration modestly — by about 8% in adults and 14% in children — meaning a 10-day cold might end roughly a day earlier ([NCBI Bookshelf summary](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK279544/); [medlineplus.gov/ency/article/002145.htm](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/002145.htm)).

A striking exception emerged in five trials (598 participants) involving marathon runners, skiers, and soldiers under subarctic conditions — extreme physical or cold-environment stress — where regular vitamin C cut cold incidence by about 50% (RR ~0.48–0.52) ([nutraingredients.com](https://www.nutraingredients.com/Article/2013/02/15/Vitamin-C-may-protect-marathon-runners-from-colds-but-what-about-the-rest-of-us/)).

**Bottom line:** For ordinary people, vitamin C doesn't prevent colds, though it may slightly shorten them; only those under severe physical/cold stress see a real preventive benefit.
